doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Synthesizers, replacing yourself and ethics
summary: Samples help composers but hurt musicians; Shear turned down low-paid singer dates and notes little solidarity among players.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Yeah. Well a lot of — well that could be synthesized sounds now. They have so many of them. Third world sounds and you can buy all that stuff that are sampled by real players that sound real. That’s good news and bad news. It’s great news for composers, but it’s bad news for the musicians. And there’s plenty of times where I had to play music in a studio that — for singers — and knowing that the singers will not hire musicians anymore because they have a prerecorded tape for their act.

I’m replacing myself exactly. Yeah. And that’s a big part of it because you’re making a paycheck for that day but you know if you didn’t do it somebody else would do it. Not that that’s the right thing to do or the wrong thing to do, it’s just a judgment call at the time. And there’s a lot of things I’ve turned down in Los Angeles in my career because I felt it wasn’t the correct thing to do.
Can you think of an example?

Well yeah. I used to get called to play horn parts in the studio for particular singers — not famous singers, just singers. And it was very low pay but it was early in the 80s so I could still pay my rent from the things I was doing. And then several years went by and it would stay the same, and several more years went by and it stayed the same, and then I asked for more money and never heard from that person again. And you’ve got to expect that. You’ve got to expect that, because there’s not a lot of solidarity among musicians. © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

There are musicians I know that say well I’ll just play for lunch, you know, just bring us some lunch in the studio and I’ll do it. For various reasons that I know, a lot of musicians, they don’t do it as their primary income. They have day jobs. They might make enough. Like I know somebody who’s a paralegal who plays an instrument, and he doesn’t really care what he makes as a musician because he makes enough as a paralegal. And this is, yeah, it’s a big problem.
